title: Checkout Got Slow at 14:00
statement: Checkout's p99 jumped from 400 ms to 3 seconds at 14:00, while its p50 stayed at 90 ms. Checkout calls six services. Exercise assumptions: every call carries a request ID; the trace of every checkout that takes 1 second or more is kept; every service logs each call it handles with its duration and the request ID, and the logs are searchable; CPU graphs exist for every server. The team wants to name the slow service in a few minutes. Which first step fits?
examples: A trace shows each service's span with its duration, so the longest span stands out.
constraints: Find which service is slow, not only that checkout is slow.
Prefer the quickest path to the answer.

approaches.name: Open several kept traces of checkouts that took 3 seconds or more since 14:00
approaches.label: best
approaches.why: A p99 of 3 seconds means at least 1 in 100 checkouts took 3 seconds or more, and all of them were kept. Each trace shows every span with its time, so the service where the time went stands out, and several traces confirm it is the same one.

approaches.name: Search the six services' logs since 14:00 for calls that took 2 seconds or more
approaches.hint: Every call is logged with its duration
approaches.label: valid
approaches.time: Longer: queries over six services' logs
approaches.why: Every call is logged with its duration, so the slow service's long calls show up, and the request IDs tie them to slow checkouts. It works, but it takes more queries than opening a few traces that already show the whole request.

approaches.name: Look for the server with the highest CPU
approaches.label: unsuitable
approaches.why: A service can be slow because it waits on something else, such as a card provider, while its CPU is low; and a busy server may be fine. CPU is a cause to check later, not a way to find the slow step.

title: An SLI for Photo Uploads
statement: A photo app wants an SLI for uploads. Users complain when an upload fails or takes more than 5 seconds. Uploads pass through a load balancer to 8 servers. Exercise assumptions: the load balancer records the result and time of every upload, including those that never reached a server; each server records only the uploads it handled; the team wants one SLI that matches what users feel, measured as close to the users as the existing records allow. Which SLI fits?
examples: An SLI is a share of good events, such as good uploads ÷ all uploads.
constraints: Count both failures and uploads slower than 5 seconds.
Include uploads that never reached a server.

approaches.name: The share of uploads that succeed within 5 seconds, from the load balancer's records
approaches.hint: Good events seen nearest the user
approaches.label: best
approaches.why: It counts both things users complain about, failures and slow uploads, and the load balancer also sees uploads that failed before any server answered.

approaches.name: Two SLIs from the load balancer's records: the share of uploads that succeed, and the share of successful uploads that finish within 5 seconds
approaches.label: valid
approaches.why: Together they count failures and slow uploads, including uploads that never reached a server, and they show which kind of problem it is. It meets the requirements but gives two numbers to track, against the stated wish for one SLI.

approaches.name: The average upload time
approaches.label: unsuitable
approaches.why: An average hides the slow uploads in the tail and ignores failures completely, so it can stay flat while users suffer. It is not a share of good events.

title: When to Wake Someone
statement: An API has an SLO of 99.9% of requests good over 30 days and handles about 50 requests per second. Exercise assumptions: a problem would use the whole month's budget within a day when 3% or more of requests are bad (a burn rate of 30); the requirement is to wake an engineer within an hour of such a problem starting, and never for a blip; a blip lasts at most 5 minutes, makes at most 20% of requests bad while it lasts, and fixes itself; blips happen several times a week. The team also prefers that paging stops soon after a problem is fixed. Which rule fits?
examples: Burn rate = bad share ÷ allowed share; at 30, a 30-day budget is gone in a day.
constraints: Page within an hour when 3% or more of requests stay bad.
Never page for a blip (at most 5 minutes, at most 20% bad).
Prefer paging that stops soon after the problem is fixed.

approaches.name: Page when 3% or more of the last hour's requests and 3% or more of the last 5 minutes' requests are bad
approaches.hint: A long window and a short one together
approaches.label: best
approaches.time: Pages within an hour; stops within 5 minutes of a fix
approaches.space: Bad-request counts per hour and per 5 minutes
approaches.why: A problem with 3% or more bad lifts the hour's share to 3% within an hour, and the last 5 minutes are above 3% too, so it pages. A blip makes at most 20% bad for 5 minutes, at most 20% × 5 ÷ 60 ≈ 1.7% of the hour, so the hour condition stays below 3% and it never pages. Once the problem is fixed, the 5-minute share drops and paging stops.

approaches.name: Page when 3% or more of the last hour's requests are bad
approaches.label: valid
approaches.time: Pages within an hour; may keep paging up to an hour after a fix
approaches.why: It pages within an hour for a real problem and never for a blip, which reaches at most about 1.7% of the hour. But after a fix the hour still contains the bad period, so the alert can keep firing for up to an hour, against the stated preference.

approaches.name: Page on every failed request
approaches.label: unsuitable
approaches.why: The SLO allows 0.1% of about 130 million requests a month, roughly 130,000 failures, to happen without harm. Paging on each one breaks the rule not to page for what the budget can absorb.
